Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Story 2 Components 3 Setup (3-6 players) 4 Game Play 5 2 Player Variant Story Look, this is a trick taking game featuring cards with numbers. There's not really a lot of theme here. But you've got to admit the name is pretty fun to say. Anyway, let's get to the game. Components 60 creature cards (6 suits, ranked 1-10) and 9 Anemone cards Setup (3-6 players) Choose one suit per player. Put any remaining cards back in the box. Shuffle the deck together and deal 10 cards to each player. Set the 9 Anemone cards within reach. The player who is reading these rules is the start player. (At 6p, remove the 1s and 10s from each suit and deal 8 to each player.) Game Play The start player plays one card face up in front of them. Every other player in clockwise order must play a card face up in front of themself in a suit that has not yet been played into the trick. If a player cannot play a suit that has not been played, they discard a card from their hand into their score pile. The highest card played wins the trick and takes all cards played into their score pile. The lowest card played takes an Anemone card, which can be added to a card in a future trick to increase its value by 1 (multiple Anemone cards may be added at once). If there is a tie for the highest or lowest value, the latter played breaks the tie. At the end of the hand, once all cards have been played, players score one point per card taken. The 3s, 5s, and 8s of each suit are worth an extra point. The player who has the lowest score at the end of the hand gains one +1 Anemone card. All Anemone cards carry over to the next hand. The Anemone cards are +1 on one side and +2 on the other. If you have a +1 and would take another, flip it instead. It now has to be played as a +2. In a 6 player game, the lowest takes a +2 and the second lowest takes a +1. If they ever run out and a player should take one, the player with the most Anemone cards must give that player one of theirs. The player with the highest score starts the next round. Play 4 rounds and the highest score wins! In case of a tie, the player with more Anemones remaining wins. 2 Player Variant Use 4 suits. Remove the 1s and 10s. Shuffle and deal 8 cards to each player and place the remaining cards in a central deck. Players take turns playing one card each into the trick until 4 cards have been played. All other rules apply, with each card needing to be a different suit. Both players draw 2 cards into their hands before playing the next trick, until the deck is empty. If there are no cards to draw, skip that step and continue playing out the rest of the hand. [Rating: 1/10] A must-not-follow that really didn't work for me. Modifying the cards means even more unintuitive ties than normal. The stakes never felt high because every trick is almost the same points. Even the dramatic round finisher from Potato Man is taken away, being short suited means just stashing more points away for yourself, but that just means one of the main gimmicks isn't that memorable.

[Rating: 3/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  We played with 6 and perhaps it does not play well at that number. Felt like there was rarely any decisions in the game. And, surprisingly, it felt like there was very rarely the opportunity to score your own card due to not being able to follow. Some of the colors can be very hard to distinguish between as well although each suit does have its own sea critter so there is always that to help figure out suit. Most times, the decision was trying to figure out who was taking the trick so we could discard our nonwinning 2 point card to someone who was not in the lead point wise 

[Rating: 3/10] The anemone twist isn’t enough to add much flair to this very basic trick-gaming game.

[Rating: 3/10] This is a forgettable trick-taking game that fails to offer anything particularly original, as the "must not follow" rule is nothing new. It's almost unplayable for colorblind players, and even difficult for non-colorblind players, as the cards look almost identical when fanned out, despite the pictures in the middle. Additionally, the dealt cards don't provide enough strategic depth, as higher cards are always objectively better than lower ones.

[Rating: 4/10] Interesting twist for a trick-taking game: you are not allowed to follow suit. Well, it sounded interesting, but the players to follow have too many options, and the last ones have nearly no influence. Intriguing, but not sure it works.

[Rating: 4/10] 4/24: No real choices, few chances ro be clever and play scoring on oneself. At the mercy of the dealth cards. I had two hands: one all middling numbers and got zero points, one with four nines and scored the highest of the hand. Card colors terrible. Maybe better with fewer than five but not interested in finding out.

[Rating: 4/10] Yawn, I play a lot of trick-takers and I usually dislike very few of them, but this one was just so mind-bogglingly boring. All the decisions and card plays felt plain obvious, the choices were often very limited as well so 90% of the time the game is completely on rails, and most “clever plays” were just based on the luck of the cards dealt. High cards are also just unequivocally better than low ones, which is just a dumb design choice in a game in which you score most of your points by winning tricks.

[Rating: 4/10] Played on BGA.  OK twist on trick taker but high cards are best, low cards are ok, and middle cards are simply bad.

[Rating: 4/10] Is it bad that it's been less than a week and I don't remember anything about this game? This works, but fails to excite.
